title: Spectrum of the Hydrogen Atom
notes: A spectrum is the ordered display of the wavelengths in a beam of radiation after dispersion by a prism or grating. An **emission** spectrum is bright lines on a dark background (excited atoms emitting); an **absorption** spectrum is dark lines on a continuous background (cool atoms removing their own characteristic wavelengths). Atomic spectra are *line* spectra — band spectra come from molecules, continuous spectra from incandescent solids.

Each line is one electron transition: the electron falls from n₂ to n₁ and emits one photon, hν = E₂ − E₁ = 13.6(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²) eV for hydrogen. Since the levels are discrete, only discrete wavelengths appear — hence a line spectrum rather than a continuous one.
• **Lyman** (n₁ = 1): to the ground level — ultraviolet; first line 121.6 nm, series limit 91.2 nm.
• **Balmer** (n₁ = 2): the only *visible* series — Hα 656.3 nm (red), Hβ 486.1 nm, Hγ 434.0 nm, Hδ 410.2 nm; limit 364.6 nm.
• Lines within a series crowd together and converge at the series limit; beyond it the spectrum becomes continuous because the atom is ionised.
### 4. Rydberg equation and the Rydberg constant

$$\bar{\nu}=\frac{1}{\lambda}=RZ^{2}\left(\frac{1}{n_{1}^{2}}-\frac{1}{n_{2}^{2}}\right),\qquad n_{2}>n_{1}$$ with R = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹ = 109 678 cm⁻¹ for hydrogen (Z = 1). Bohr's theory *derived* R = 2π²me⁴/h³c, turning Rydberg's empirical formula into theory — the model's greatest success.
• Spectral analysis identifies elements: each element has a unique line pattern, used in chemistry labs, metallurgy, forensics and pollution monitoring.
• Astronomy: composition, temperature and motion (Doppler shift) of stars are read from hydrogen lines; the 21 cm hydrogen line maps interstellar gas.
• Technology: atomic emission/absorption spectroscopy (AAS, ICP), flame tests, He–Ne gas lasers (632.8 nm) and spectrometer calibration all rest on hydrogen-like energy levels.
• Frank–Hertz and discharge-tube experiments confirm discrete energy levels and the Bohr energy expression.

The Bohr/Rydberg picture gives series positions but not line *fine structure* (Hα is really a doublet), relative intensities, or splitting in magnetic (Zeeman) and electric (Stark) fields; beyond hydrogen it needs multi-electron and relativistic corrections.
confusion: ❌ The Balmer series lies in the ultraviolet. ✅ Balmer (n₁ = 2) is visible; Lyman (n₁ = 1) is UV and Paschen onward are IR.
❌ A ground-state hydrogen atom can emit a line. ✅ Emission needs excitation first; the ground state can only absorb.
❌ Within a series the lines get farther apart. ✅ They crowd together and converge at the series limit.
❌ Absorption lines mean the atom lost energy. ✅ The atom absorbs exactly the photons matching its level gaps, so those wavelengths are missing from the transmitted beam.
❌ Every line requires n₂ − n₁ = 1. ✅ Any n₂ > n₁ gives a line; the number of lines from level n is n(n − 1)/2.

universalFacts: Hα = 656.3 nm (red) is the first Balmer line; Lyman limit = 91.2 nm; Balmer limit = 364.6 nm.
The Balmer series was discovered first (1885) because it alone lies in the visible region.
examples: **Problem:** Wavelength of the first Balmer line (n = 3 → 2). **Solution:** 1/λ = 1.097×10⁷(1/4 − 1/9) = 1.524×10⁶ m⁻¹ → λ = 656 nm (Hα).
**Problem:** Energy of the photon for n = 4 → 2. **Solution:** ΔE = 13.6(1/4 − 1/16) = 2.55 eV; λ = 1240/2.55 ≈ 486 nm (Hβ).

summary: An emission spectrum shows bright lines on a dark background and an absorption spectrum dark lines on a continuous background; atomic spectra are line spectra, band spectra coming from molecules and continuous spectra from incandescent solids. In hydrogen each line is a single electron transition, hν = E₂ − E₁ = 13.6(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²) eV, so discrete levels give discrete wavelengths. The series are named by the lower level n₁: Lyman (n₁ = 1, UV, limit 91.2 nm), Balmer (n₁ = 2, the only visible series — Hα 656.3 nm, Hβ 486.1 nm, Hγ 434.0 nm, Hδ 410.2 nm, limit 364.6 nm), and Paschen, Brackett and Pfund in the infrared. Within a series the lines crowd together and converge at the series limit, where ionisation begins and the spectrum turns continuous. The Rydberg equation, 1/λ = RZ²(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²) with R = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹, was derived by Bohr, and the pattern is used for elemental analysis, stellar astronomy and lasers.
importantConcepts: Emission (bright lines on dark ground) versus absorption (dark lines on a continuous source)

importantStatements: The Balmer series is the only hydrogen series in the visible region; Lyman is ultraviolet and Paschen onward infrared.
Within a series the lines crowd closer together and converge at the series limit, they do not spread apart.
A ground-state hydrogen atom can absorb but cannot emit a Balmer line — emission needs prior excitation.
The number of spectral lines from a single excited level n is n(n − 1)/2.
Bohr's derivation of R turned Rydberg's empirical formula into theory — the model's greatest success.

keyPoints: Discrete energy levels are the reason the spectrum is lines, not a continuum.
Hα = 656.3 nm (red) is the first Balmer line; Balmer limit = 364.6 nm, Lyman limit = 91.2 nm.
The number of lines possible from level n is n(n − 1)/2.
λ(nm) = 1240/ΔE(eV) converts a transition energy into a wavelength.
The Balmer series was found first (1885) because it alone is visible.
specialNotes: Absorption lines mark missing wavelengths, not energy lost by the atom: the atom keeps exactly the photons matching its level gaps.
Beyond the series limit the electron is free, so the spectrum becomes continuous — the limit is the ionisation threshold.
The Bohr picture gives line positions only; fine structure (Hα is a doublet), intensities and Zeeman/Stark splitting need quantum mechanics.
